content:
My thoughts on formalization in physics

TL;DR – Physics can only make progress because we throw out all formalism that’s not essential to the problem at hand. PhysLib should reflect that.

Einstein is alleged to have said ““Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler.”. I suspect those were not his actual words but his meaning was “Throw out everything except what is essential to the physics”. I think this is a good guiding principle for formalizing physics.

To turn this into reality it’s helpful to consider real use cases. I believe if PhysLib is truly to become a definitive source of knowledge, valid use cases include:

  • A high-school student studying maths / physics / computer science can follow the derivation of pendulum motion
  • An undergraduate learning relativity can follow the derivation of Special Relativity starting from the assumption of invariance of a light ray.
  • A graduate student can follow the calculation of the chiral anomaly and the anomaly-cancellation conditions for consistent chiral field theories.

Specifically taking the first of these, I think if you asked a professor of mathematical physics to explain pendulum motion, they would draw the diagram, resolve forces and apply Newton’s 2nd law just like a high school student. What they would do beyond a high-school student is realize the phase space is a circle and that there are non-periodic solutions that stop at theta = pi.

What they would (hopefully) not do is start with a bunch of lemmas around existence of derivatives etc etc because that would actually make the physics inaccessible to the vast majority of the audience that are capable of understanding a pendulum.

My 3 examples have increasing levels of required formalism. For the second you need a notion of transformation laws and invariance. For the 3rd you need to understand (as much as anyone does) how to regularise a field theory and consistently take the limit as the regulator vanishes. But at each level the formalism is just what’s required to solve the problem.

What quantities do we actually deal with in physics?

If I write down a “variable” (in CS language) in physics it generally has

  • A domain (space and time or their relativistic combination)
  • A set of transformation laws under symmetries
  • A set of transformation laws under gauge changes

For example the classical electric field is defined over (space + time), transforms as a vector under spatial rotations and picks up a \grad \phi under a gauge change.

There may be additional properties such as being complex (e.g. spinors). There will be other “variables” such as total energy that don’t depend on the domain.

By default I’ll assume that things are real and infinitely differentiable unless I explicitly say otherwise. When we write down an electric field we should be able to assume differentiability unless there is an explicit obstruction like a point charge or conducting boundary. I think PhysLib should be able to abstract away these assumptions so we can focus on the content.

Lean code

We’ve spent the last few decades watching coding languages evolve from the hieroglyphic (COBOL, Fortran) that required extensive external documentation to the point where modern code is self-documenting and should be readable almost like a piece of text. Lean is not like that at present, and this may well serve formal mathematics well. I suspect Physics would be served better by code that reads like

expand_brackets (<expression>)

integrate(<integrand>, 3dspace)

normal_order (<expression>)

and if this were accompanied by the ability to pretty-print a latex derivation of the lemma being proved we’d have easily readable code with direct linkage to how people learn the subject.
Interesting perspective @Art Mountain, could I ask you to elaborate on your suggestion for lean code using a concrete example :)

To turn this into reality it’s helpful to consider real use cases. I believe if PhysLib is truly to become a definitive source of knowledge, valid use cases include:

I agree with this. I think the difficulty and fun question is to work out how to best do this in practice.
This is raw output from Claude code. I gave it this prompt

Please can you generate a lean module that describes classical dynamics - force, mass, acceleration and the SUVAT equations that school children learn? I'd like this done so that the lean code can be read by a capable 17 year old who nis taking maths and physics at high school. Please keep formalism to the minimum required to get the physics correct and provide a valuable learning resource for a school age student

Some parts of the file are good, some bad. To strat with I'd put the 3 definitions v = ds/dt, a = dv/dt and Newton's 2nd law at the top (this file actually takes the displacement s = ut + at^2 / 2 as an input, it doesn't derive it by integration)
But to answer the actual question, what makes this hard to read and use?...

To start with the keywords in lean. I'm no lean expert. I don't know if it's possible to alias keywords like it is in C++. I'd love to see these aliases
unfold(...) -> replace_with_definition(...)
rw(...) -> apply_lemma(...)
norm_num[...] -> simplify_with_arithmetic[...]

That would make the code far more readable. Another barrier to the student would be the use of the keyword "ring". It's a nice mathematical generalization but is not required to do classical mechanics (or indeed most of modern theoretical physics)

My final example is

-- the derivative of t (with respect to t) is 1
have hid : HasDerivAt (fun x : ℝ => x) 1 t := hasDerivAt_id t

I appreciate we need to be careful whether a derivative exists. After all even in classical mechanics we get delta-functions, e.g. the acceleration in an elastic collision. But ideally we could replace this very abstract formalsm with a

derivative(f x, x)

This could wrap an object which know about the special points / discontinuities. It will be too simple for more advanced applications but would provide a way of simplifying the code when those subtleties aren't important.

I believe there are multiple things being conflated here. I will attempt to explain my thoughts on this, but I can't guarantee they are fully coherent and this is something I'm actively thinking about.

"Formalism" is a vague word can could mean a multitude of things. It is already unclear what it points to specifically in mathematics, but physics adds an additional layer of confusion. Is it (1) a framework of encoding physics in a formal language, (2) the mathematical rigour of doing physics, or (3) the presentation and syntax of the content? These point to quite different considerations when we perform "formalisation".

I interpret what you saying about physics progress is about (2), where in theorizing and pedagogy we often defer rigour in favour of "intuition". I agree with the sentiment that we should support the working style of physicists where we can focus on the more physically interesting statements, rather than having to fight through the proofs of less interesting ones, e.g. differentiability conditions. However, I would argue the solution isn't to omit them, but to provide sufficient API and automation around them, so they can be discharged by the machine (in the differentiability case, in the ideal world everything would just be fun_prop and not interfere with the main arguments). After all, by the very definition of a formalisation is to state things rigorously, and if we omit these then I don't see why do we even need to use a theorem prover like lean compared to writing in prose, e.g. a wikipedia/nlab page. The power of a theorem prover is precisely that it would not accept statements that do not meet all conditions.

To me your concern seems to be more of that of (3), the presentation of it. This is perfectly doable in Lean, e.g. the textbook Mechanics of Proof introduces many custom tactics and aliases, and you are more than welcome to develop your own exposition that is high-school friendly. In fact I think that would be a great contribution to the lean for physics community and encourage you to experiment with that. However, I don't believe physlib is necessarily aligned with this goal. Physlib should aim for generality and "correctness" in the sense that the assumptions are made explicit to ensure the theorems and statements do reflect their usage in physics without ambiguity. I would argue that the boundaries of applications and the assumptions behind models are an often neglected but equally important part of physics, and the justification of a physical model is often mediated by exactly these conditions.

now about your claude-generated file, there are many issues with it, but I think the main issue is that this way of "formalising physics" seems to view lean as merely an arithmetic checker, and I think this is a common pitfall that does a huge disservice to both lean and physics. Physics isn't just about algebraic relationships between variables, and lean can express much more than that. Stripped of the condition under which they hold, the SUVAT equations stop being physics and become arithmetic. A high-school student could very well do all the arithmetic but that says nothing about the understanding of physics behind it, and to go further you'll soon find out the thing you want to get rid of is fundamental to the physics content.
